ch10 - Real, This Book.md
chapters.relation: The volume's introduction is written in Elliot's paranoid voice, doubting whether the book, the reader, or reality itself exist. It lays out the questions the essays will tackle: fsociety's hack of the Evil Corporation, whether it was political ideology or revenge for the corporation killing Elliot's and Darlene's father, whether either motive (or hacking in general) can be justified, and what order could survive after the financial system falls.

chapters.file: ch11 - I. We’re All Living in Each Other’s Paranoia.md
ch12 - 1. The Deed of F’ing Society.md
chapters.relation: Rocha reads fsociety's 5/9 logic-bomb attack on E Corp as anarchist 'propaganda of the deed' - a shocking act meant to wake people from their comfortable slumber inside hierarchy - and positions it between Alexander Berkman's violent anarchism (mirroring Phillip Price's 'bullet in the right place') and Gandhi's nonviolent self-suffering, quoting satyagraha and the older Goldman's rejection of violence. He then runs the hack through just war theory's four questions (necessity, proportionality, justification, effectiveness), noting that wiping the debt records also destroyed savings and indirectly got people like Gideon killed, and that fsociety, as Trenton says, never paints the alternative society - so the reader is left to answer whether the deed was justified.

chapters.file: ch13 - 2. If I Don’t Listen to My Imaginary Friend, Why the Fuck Should I Listen to Yours.md
chapters.relation: Kreider stages a chat between Plato and Aristotle about the show. On Plato's account, mimesis is an imitation of an imitation of the Forms, so Elliot's imaginary friend, his fake persona with Krista, and the Mr. Robot personality are intellectually and morally dangerous deceptions that let him commit terrorism without his rational self's consent; yet the Republic's censored poetry for the auxiliaries explains how fsociety's masked videos teach true beliefs, and how Elliot uses the fictional Mr. Robot to educate himself toward ideas he already knew were right. Aristotle's Poetics then defends imitation as natural and instructive - the show is a cautionary tragedy, and the Mr. Robot crutch is how Elliot eventually steps up to claim responsibility.

chapters.file: ch14 - 3. Click Bait for Black Fish.md
chapters.relation: Porot reads Elliot through Berlin's positive liberty: people are enslaved to their lower selves - the 'daemons' of addiction and primal urge Elliot describes in 'eps1.3_da3m0ns.mp4' - and freedom requires a contract in which an external force holds you to your higher self. Elliot writes such contracts with Shayla over his drugs and imagines Mr. Robot as the paternalistic enforcer who pushes him off the pier when he breaks his word, while corporations run the reverse contract, 'hacking' people from within through addictive sugar, clickbait, and advertising. The black fish dream crystallizes this: everyone at the office devours the confined fish of reverse-contract slavery while Elliot alone eats Pop's pie - freedom through the father figure of Mr. Robot.

chapters.file: ch15 - II. Control Is an Illusion.md
ch16 - 4. The End of Privacy.md
chapters.relation: Brake reads Mr. Robot through Thomas More's Utopia: Hythloday's 'conspiracy of the rich' matches E Corp's Washington Township cover-up, his attacks on private property echo Elliot's monologue about property and money, and the island with 'nothing private anywhere' frames the provocative idea that the veil of privacy shelters corporate injustice that only lawbreaking - fsociety's hacks, Manning, Snowden, Assange - can lift into daylight. Yet More splits himself between idealist Hythloday and pragmatic More, and the messy aftermath of the 5/9 hack shows that utopian dreams implemented without caution can become nightmares.

chapters.file: ch17 - 5. We Become the Grid.md
chapters.relation: Ketcham updates Hobbes for the network age: the grid born of ARPANET and Cold War mutual destruction has devolved into a new state of nature, out of which a coming 'Leviathan' - the one percent of the one percent - will rule invisibly by curating your memories, your purchases, your spouse, and whole countries like the diamond-republic fable. Invoking Descartes's evil demon and Heidegger's ready-to-hand, he asks whether we have become the grid, an external brain we can no longer control, and concludes that Elliot, the rogue 'Ebola' who hacks for justice rather than profit, is exactly the loose cannon Leviathan would quarantine.

chapters.file: ch18 - 6. Who Has the Power.md
chapters.relation: Samuelson uses Foucault to dismantle Phillip Price's creed of being 'the most powerful person in the room': power is not a possession but an operation. Elliot's men in black and the FBI's surveillance are disciplinary power - Bentham's panopticon realized in Allsafe's cube farm and the internet itself - while Angela's fight over the Washington Township leak is a struggle with biopower that no sovereign can be punished for, and Whiterose's knowledge is power-knowledge that operates anonymously no matter who holds it. If Foucault is right, Price, Mr. Robot, and Zheng are mere conduits, and no one will ever be the most powerful person in the room.

chapters.file: ch19 - III. They All Think I’m the Ringleader.md
ch20 - 7. What Kind of Revolutionary Is Mr. Robot.md
chapters.relation: Ralston traces Mr. Robot's hacktivist philosophy to David Graeber's anarchism behind Occupy Wall Street and to Anonymous's 'moralfags' who hack for a higher cause (Project Chanology as the template for fsociety), then stages the Dewey-Trotsky debate on means and ends: Trotsky's 'Their Morals and Ours' lets the end justify any means, while Dewey's means-end continuum demands experimental, democratic means suited to the end. The verdict: Mr. Robot's ends are anarchist and his means pragmatist - he will frame Terry Colby and risk lives at Steel Mountain, but rejects means like actual slavery that would betray the movement's own ideal of liberation.

chapters.file: ch21 - 8. Mr. Robot, Mad Son of Noir.md
chapters.relation: Hoyt places Mr. Robot in the film noir tradition born when world war proved Nietzsche's point that God is dead: as with Bogart's Spade turning in Brigid in The Maltese Falcon, the noir hero's task is existential self-definition - guarding integrity in a world without truth, justice, or absolute meaning. But where classic noir blamed gangsters, neo-noir from Chinatown through Fight Club to Mr. Robot points at capitalism and unbeatable conspiracies (Price apparently able to bend the federal government itself), and the show's cold blue offices and 'shortsighting' framings show characters breaking under the pressure of choices no space protects.

chapters.file: ch22 - 9. What Elliot Doesn’t Know Won’t Hurt You (Or Will It ).md
chapters.relation: Greene argues Elliot is in the worst possible position for a knower: Descartes's skeptical scenarios of madness, dreams, and the evil demon apply to everyone, but hit Elliot harder through morphine and ecstasy hallucinations, lucid dreams indistinguishable from waking (as Whiterose suggests), and a dissociative disorder so severe he spends months in prison believing he lives at his mother's house - with Mr. Robot even hiding facts from him, blocking the Socratic 'know thyself.' Yet by the Meno's knowledge problem he may be no worse off: he still catches the pedophile ring and brings down E Corp, so the hero of the show succeeds without knowledge.

chapters.file: ch23 - IV. Politics Is for Puppets.md
ch24 - 10. If It Isn’t Justified Is It Still My Revolution.md
chapters.relation: Writing as a guilt-ridden fsociety member haunted by James Plouffe's on-air suicide, Altmann tests the 5/9 revolution against three theorists: Burke's conservatism condemns all revolution as destruction of social tradition (and fsociety's blackout chaos and Susan Jacobs's death seem to prove him right), while Marx's class struggle between E Corp's bourgeoisie and the indebted proletariat makes revolution the only exit from history's cycle. Kai Nielsen's condition - revolution is justified only when no other recourse exists - settles it: Angela's failed attempt to reform E Corp from within shows non-revolutionary change is impossible, so the author keeps fighting 'with a keyboard whose clacking is endless.'

chapters.file: ch25 - 11. The Gods Are Dead and Elliot Has Killed Them.md
chapters.relation: Robison-Greene reads Elliot's chapel monologue - 'If I don't listen to my imaginary friend, why the fuck should I listen to yours?' - as a Problem of Evil argument: an omniscient, omnipotent, omnibenevolent God is incompatible with the unnecessary suffering of his father's death and of massive income inequality. The 'gods' Elliot kills are also Mr. Robot ('like all gods their madness takes you prisoner') and the religion of materialism, and Nietzsche supplies the blueprint for what follows: the Genealogy's slave revolt in values as the model for fsociety's uprising, and the Parable of the Madman plus the Ubermensch to cast Elliot-as-Mr. Robot as the creator of new values - though unlike Nietzsche's slaves, the oppressed here are complicit in their own subordination.

chapters.file: ch26 - 12. Why Angela Drops the Whistle.md
chapters.relation: Jones asks why Angela flees the Nuclear Regulatory Commission at the exact moment she could expose the Washington Township cover-up, and answers with the real world of whistleblowing: Chelsea Manning's thirty-five-year sentence shows the legal peril, and the Rasmussen poll branding Manning a traitor plus the Enron fallout show the court of public opinion demonizes whistleblowers. Tribal survival instincts make insiders punish anyone who drops the tribe's secrets, and coworkers must condemn the whistleblower to preserve their own self-worth against the mirror of their silence - so even a legally protected, morally sound Angela backs away.

chapters.file: ch27 - V. Power Belongs to the People Who Take It.md
ch28 - 13. How to Become a Revolutionary.md
chapters.relation: Luzecky and Elsby argue traditional political philosophy cannot describe Mr. Robot's revolution - a leader who calls himself a computer virus - and turn to Deleuze and Guattari: capitalism runs on coded flows of money, labor, and desire (taxation existing to insert the state into our lives), and hackers become revolutionaries by interrupting those flows. Elliot is a 'nomadic war-machine' whose non-segmented space makes his power literally beyond measure, and the true revolution turns out to be personal and affirmative: embracing the countless fucked-up desires you are instead of accepting the coded range of acceptable behavior.

chapters.file: ch29 - 14. Is E Corp an Evil Person.md
chapters.relation: Wood asks what E Corp ontologically is: on Plato's theory, it would participate in a Form of Corporation, while Aristotle's primary substances show E Corp is not an individual at all - just a name for ways people interact. Corporate personhood (from 1819 contract rights through Citizens United and Hobby Lobby) makes it a legal person whose responsibility diffuses 'almost to the point of evaporation,' and Kant's humanity formula explains the unease: a legal fiction with no intentions or dignity can never respect persons as ends, which is why Angela's quest for a moral 'who' behind Washington Township ends only with the two ordinary executives Price hands her.

chapters.file: ch30 - 15. Reset Virtues.md
chapters.relation: Doll argues Elliot approximates Aristotelian virtue despite his vices: he craves eudaimonia, uses practical wisdom to recognize the harm the 5/9 hack caused innocent people ('I'll own it all'), and habituates himself against vice by confessing, exposing Ray's website, and restraining Mr. Robot even at the cost of Adderall binges and prison. Leon's 'existence could be beautiful, or it could be ugly, but that's on you' frames the choice of a life to fight for, and Krista's counsel leads Elliot to the golden mean of a 'handshake' with Mr. Robot - integrating the two identities rather than annihilating one - while the viewer serves as the if/then programming keeping him virtuous.

chapters.file: ch31 - VI. Is Any of It Real.md
ch32 - 16. 0n-keeping-everyb0dy-1n-the-d4rk.docx.md
chapters.relation: Fallis treats Mr. Robot as a hidden war of epistemic adversaries - not Descartes's deceiving demon mostly, but combatants who keep each other in the dark. Testing Sissela Bok's definition of secret-keeping against counterexamples (Elliot keeps Krista in the dark just by holding his tongue; not reporting breakfast is not keeping people in the dark), he adopts Chisholm's 'negative deception' - intentionally causing a lack of true belief - and resolves the paradox of self-deception through the show's split centers of agency: the Mr. Robot part of Elliot's mind deceives the Elliot part about Tyrell, Stage Two, and prison itself.

chapters.file: ch33 - 17. Our Lying Eyes.md
chapters.relation: Wood asks how Elliot - and we, who see only what he sees - can know anything, and contrasts two empiricisms: Locke's white-paper mind furnished by ideas copied from mind-independent objects, which explains Mr. Robot as perceptual error, and Berkeley's idealism, on which only ideas and their divine cause exist, which makes Elliot's unshared hallucination of Mr. Robot dangerously hard to distinguish from reality. Consistency of perception is the only test left, and it fails Elliot until the pier video proves no one pushed him - and fails us again when his cozy Season Two routine turns out to be prison.

chapters.file: ch34 - 18. Psycho-Politics in a Burnout Society.md
chapters.relation: Pagnoni Berns and Aguilar read the show through Byung-Chul Han's philosophy: in the transparency society everyone stacks their life online - Krista is transparent to Elliot because her password is Dylan and her birthday, while he stays opaque - and psycho-politics replaces Foucauldian punishment with seduction, a digital panopticon (Operation Berenstain, Minister Zhang) whose inmates voluntarily build it. Elliot's attention deficits, Tyrell's breakdown over Sharon Knowles's corpse, and Gideon's fatigue embody the burnout society's neuronal violence, and even fsociety reproduces the systemic coercion it fights, leaving 'real life' only outside the system.

chapters.file: ch35 - 19. Please Tell Me You’re Seeing This Too.md
chapters.relation: Ehrnberger argues Mr. Robot hooks us like a Trojan horse: Todorov's 'ambiguity of the fantastic' - the irresolvable hesitation over whether Elliot's world is real or imagined - makes his unreliable narration endlessly rewatchable, which is how a mainstream network show smuggles in Adorno's critique of the very culture industry that airs it. Adorno explains the sedation Elliot decries ('we wanna be sedated') and why enlightenment reverts to mythology - meritocracy, consumerism, digital connection as modern myths we no longer recognize as myths - while Ehrenberg's 'illness of responsibility' explains why freed people retreat into the comfort of those myths rather than bear freedom's weight.

holes.name: Propaganda of the Deed
holes.what: The anarchist doctrine that shocking public acts, violent or not, serve as propaganda that wakes the masses from social slumber and forces society to change.
holes.why: Chapter 12 frames the entire 5/9 hack as propaganda of the deed, positioning fsociety between Berkman's violent anarchism and Gandhi's self-suffering.

holes.name: Mimesis (art as imitation)
holes.what: Plato's doctrine that art imitates physical things, which themselves imitate the Forms, making art an imitation of an imitation - against Aristotle's defense of imitation as natural and instructive.
holes.why: Chapter 13's whole assessment of Elliot's imaginary friend, the Mr. Robot persona, and fsociety's masks turns on the Plato-Aristotle debate over mimesis.

holes.name: Thomas More
holes.what: Author of Utopia (1516), whose character Hythloday argues that private property and money make justice impossible and imagines a commonwealth with no privacy.
holes.why: Chapter 16 reads Elliot's hacktivism and the case for tearing down the veil of privacy almost entirely through More's Utopia and its conspiracy of the rich.

holes.name: Biopower
holes.what: Foucault's notion of modern power exercised over the life and bodies of populations through institutions and norms rather than by a sovereign's decree.
holes.why: Chapter 18 uses biopower to explain why no one is punished for the Washington Township leak that killed Angela's mother.

holes.name: Leon Trotsky
holes.what: Marxist revolutionary who argued in 'Their Morals and Ours' that revolutionary ends justify whatever means the class struggle requires.
holes.why: Chapter 20 stages the Dewey-Trotsky means-ends debate as the key test of whether Mr. Robot's hacktivism is justified.

holes.name: Edmund Burke
holes.what: Founder of modern conservatism who condemned the French Revolution, holding that society is an organism that must change only gradually through its traditions.
holes.why: Chapter 24 uses Burke as the conservative condemnation against which Marx's and Nielsen's justifications of fsociety's revolution are tested.

holes.name: Kai Nielsen
holes.what: Political philosopher who argues Marxist revolution is justified only when no other course of action could achieve the same end.
holes.why: Chapter 24 adopts Nielsen's no-recourse condition - confirmed by Angela's failed inside reform of E Corp - as the decisive justification of the 5/9 hack.

holes.name: Whistleblowing
holes.what: An insider's report of an organization's illegal or immoral conduct to outside authorities or the public, with its attendant legal protections and social costs.
holes.why: Chapter 26's entire explanation of why Angela abandons the Washington Township disclosure turns on the ethics and risks of whistleblowing.

holes.name: The Nomadic War-Machine
holes.what: Deleuze and Guattari's figure of an exterior, non-segmented collective defined by its capacity to betray the state's codes and interrupt capitalist flows.
holes.why: Chapter 28 models Elliot and fsociety as a nomadic war-machine whose revolution attacks limitation itself rather than any particular institution.

holes.name: Corporate Personhood
holes.what: The legal doctrine treating corporations as persons bearing rights and liabilities even though they lack the intentionality and dignity of natural persons.
holes.why: Chapter 29's question of whether E Corp can be an evil or morally responsible person is exactly the problem of corporate personhood.

holes.name: Deception and Keeping in the Dark
holes.what: Intentionally causing someone to have a false belief (deception) or to lack a true belief (keeping them in the dark), including the paradox of self-deception.
holes.why: Chapter 32 analyzes Mr. Robot's hacker war as applied epistemology built on defining deception versus keeping people in the dark.

holes.name: Byung-Chul Han
holes.what: Korean-German philosopher of the transparency society, psycho-politics, and the burnout society, where power works through seduction and self-exploitation rather than repression.
holes.why: Chapter 34 reads Elliot, Tyrell, and Gideon as embodiments of Han's burnout society and its digital panopticon.

holes.name: The Fantastic (Todorov)
holes.what: Tzvetan Todorov's literary category of the unresolved hesitation between realistic and imaginary explanations of the events narrated.
holes.why: Chapter 35 argues the fantastic's ambiguity in Elliot's unreliable narration is precisely how Mr. Robot hooks its audience.
